notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 96. A few gaps first:

- **Sources I couldn't read:** I found nothing from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Orthodox sources (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out.
- **NET Bible notes:** the NET page I opened for v. 10 showed no notes.
- **Tradition labels:** where I call a writer Baptist, Reformed and so on, that label is my own and doesn't come from the pages. On these pages, the clearest split between traditions is over end times, in vv. 10 and 13.

---

## Background

- **Shape of the psalm:** Guzik sees it widening in circles: first God's people, then all nations, then creation itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
- **Author:** No author is named in the Hebrew. But the psalm makes up the middle of the song David sang when the ark came into Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:23-33), which suggests David wrote it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
- **Title in the Greek Old Testament:** It reads "When the house was built after the exile." Bible.org's sermon notes the psalm shares many themes with Isaiah 40–66. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-96-worshiping-witnessing-waiting
- **Reading the whole psalm about Christ:** Clarke says most Christian writers, old and new, read it as a prophecy of Christ's kingdom, growing as the Gentiles join and ending with his coming to judge. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-13.html
- **Spurgeon's collection:** It calls the psalm a "millennial anthem," fitting the time when Christ reigns over a willing human race. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps096.cfm

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - A "new song" doesn't have to be new music. It comes from seeing God's love and grace afresh. Clarke (quoted by Guzik) takes "new" to mean especially excellent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - "All the earth" shows the LORD is not a local god meant only for Israel. Guzik links the verse to its fulfilment in Revelation 5:9. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Matthew Henry: the new song will never grow old or out of date. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_096.cfm
  - Benson ties the new song to the Messiah's coming, the new covenant and the calling of the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-1.htm
- **Modern scholarship:**
  - The Cambridge Bible traces the line to Isaiah 42:10. It links the "fresh mercies" to Israel's return from Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-1.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary notes this line is missing from 1 Chronicles 16. It suggests the psalm was later reworked for a "new" occasion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-1.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):**
  - The "old song" is the desire of the flesh; the new song is the love of God, tied to Christ's "new commandment." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm
  - Reading the Greek title, Augustine says the "house" being built is the church spreading across the whole world. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Clarke says the Hebrew is strong: "Preach the Gospel of his salvation." The Greek Old Testament likewise says "evangelize." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-96.html
  - Barnes takes "day to day" as constant praise, every morning and evening. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-96.html
  - Spurgeon: the gospel reveals God more clearly than creation or providence do, so praise should flow most of all for salvation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps096.cfm
  - Gill (Baptist) applies the verse especially to gospel ministers, preaching one Lord's Day after another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-2.htm
- **Possible hint of the Trinity:** Gill notes some see the Trinity in "LORD" being said three times. The Catholic Haydock commentary sees the Trinity in the switch between plural and singular. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-2.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/psalms-95.html

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Boice (quoted by Guzik): the Hebrew word for glory, *kabod*, means something weighty or impressive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - A writer in Spurgeon's collection notes the psalm calls the same thing "salvation," then "glory," then "wonders." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps096.cfm
  - Bible.org: worship is both the goal of missions and its foundation. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-96-worshiping-witnessing-waiting
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Declare *His* honour, not your own. He also turns the verse against groups that refuse fellowship with the church worldwide. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm
- **Modern caution:** Pulpit's sermon notes admit that reading this as missions is an application. The returning exile, they say, didn't have the conversion of the nations in mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/96.htm

**v. 4**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Guzik: the praise is grounded in God's real greatness, not empty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Barnes: even if the pagan gods were real, they would be local and lesser, with no claim to worship from the whole world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-4.htm
  - Gill widens "gods" to include angels and earthly rulers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-4.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** He applies "great, and cannot worthily be praised" to Christ, who made himself small. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm

**v. 5**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - The Hebrew word for idols, *elilim*, mocks the word for God, *elohim*. It means roughly "nothings." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - VanGemeren (quoted by Guzik): the gods are fakes because the LORD alone made the heavens. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Ellicott: "nothings" could not make the heavens, only the LORD could. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-5.htm
  - Barnes: real things that were worshipped, like the sun or stars, still had no existence *as gods*. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-5.htm
- **Older Jewish translations:** Keil and Delitzsch note the Greek Old Testament has "demons" here (compare 1 Corinthians 10:20). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-5.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Following that Greek reading, he says the nations' gods are devils. He adds that "the Lord made the heavens" lifts Christ above both gods and heavens. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm

**v. 6**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Benson: honour and majesty shine from God's face, like beams from the Sun of righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-4.htm
  - Clarke asks whether this means the glory-cloud that went before the ark. He notes "strength" and "beauty" are words used for the ark in Psalm 78:61. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-96.html
  - Barnes: the power to reform the world comes from the "sanctuary," meaning the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-96.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** His Latin text reads "confession and beauty." He says to confess your sins first, and beauty follows. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm

**v. 7**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - To "give" or "ascribe" means to recognise what is already true of God. It does not add anything to him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Cassiodorus (quoted by Spurgeon): "kindreds of the peoples" includes foreigners and outsiders, so no one is excluded because of where they come from. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps096.cfm

**v. 8**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Clarke: the glory due to God is a debt, and a debt must be paid. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps096.cfm
  - Guzik sees a hint of the Trinity in the threefold "ascribe." He adds that true worship often shows itself in sacrifice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Barnes: the word for offering (*minchah*) usually means a bloodless thank-offering. The Cambridge Bible: it is the gift subjects bring their lord as a sign of submission. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-8.htm
- **Protestant readings of "offering":**
  - Gill (Baptist): not the ceremonial sacrifices, which are ended. It means our bodies, a broken heart, giving to the poor and to ministry, prayer and praise — or best of all, Christ's sacrifice received by faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-8.htm
  - The Geneva Bible (Reformed): offer yourselves wholly to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-8.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The gift to bring is a humble, contrite heart. The proud come in empty-handed. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm

**v. 9**
- **"Splendour of holiness" vs "holy attire":**
  - Guzik reads it as the beauty of God's own holiness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Spurgeon applies it to worship: God doesn't care about fine buildings or clothing, only moral and spiritual beauty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps096.cfm
  - Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible translate "holy attire." Keil and Delitzsch compare it to the wedding garment in Jesus' parable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-9.htm
- **"Tremble":** Barnes: the word first meant to writhe, then to tremble. It describes deep awe at God's presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-96.html
- **Gill:** The verse pictures subjects bowing before an Eastern king. He applies the verse to the "latter day" when nations fear the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-9.htm

**v. 10 (main point of disagreement)**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Guzik: the Lord reigns whether people recognise it or not, and one day his reign will be openly established. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Ellicott: "Jehovah has become King" was the cry of the return from exile, good news for the whole world. https://biblehub.com/psalms/96-10.htm
  - Calvin (Reformed): there is no true order in the world until God sets up his throne among people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-10.html
- **When does this reign come? Where views differ:**
  - Matthew Henry and Gill (shown together on StudyLight): judging here means ruling. It points mainly to Christ's *first* coming and his kingdom spreading through the gospel, though it can extend to the last judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-10.html
  - Coffman: the reign began at Pentecost and is happening now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-10.html
  - Constable (labelled dispensational on the page): Christ will judge fairly when he *returns* and sets up his millennial kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-10.html
- **What is "the world" that "cannot be moved"?**
  - Clarke notes many take it to mean the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-10.html
  - Gill denies it means the physical world, which will pass away. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/psalms/96-10.html
- **Ancient variant, "reigned from the wood":**
  - Augustine uses "the Lord has reigned from the wood," meaning the cross. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801096.htm
  - Clarke: Justin Martyr quoted it this way and accused the Jews of removing it. But no Hebrew manuscript or ancient translation has it, and Jerome and Eusebius never mention it. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/psalms/96-10.html

**vv. 11–12**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Righteous judgment is good news for creation and for the oppressed. Guzik links this to Romans 8:21. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
  - Bible.org: creation now groans under the curse, waiting for redemption. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-96-worshiping-witnessing-waiting
  - VanGemeren: "trees of the forest" suggests wild land or thick jungle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-96/
- **Modern scholarship:** Keil and Delitzsch note that v. 11 happens to spell out divine names acrostically. They doubt this was intended. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-10.htm

**v. 13**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Ellicott: "he cometh, he cometh" is said twice out of joy. https://biblehub.com/psalms/96-13.htm
  - Gill, following Jerome: the repetition may point to Christ's first and second comings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-13.htm
  - Barnes: this happens now wherever the gospel rules in hearts, and will be complete when Christ returns. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-13.htm
  - Bible.org: "faithfulness" means God's judgment will not be arbitrary. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-96-worshiping-witnessing-waiting
- **Judgment as rule, not just punishment:**
  - Cambridge Bible: the main idea is governing, though that includes punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-13.htm
  - Pulpit, quoting Hengstenberg: a "gracious judging," not mainly punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/96-13.htm
  - Pulpit's sermon notes say the idea of God judging continually is replacing the "older idea" of a single final judgment day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/96.htm
- **Premillennial view:** Constable calls the verse one of the clearest statements that God will rule *on earth*, in his Son, at the Second Coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-13.html
- **Catholic (Haydock and Clarke):** Clarke records that the church fathers took "he cometh" as the Incarnation. The second line is the coming that frightens the wicked but comforts the righteous. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/96-13.html
